## Incident Report — MTA 2024-07-30 Traffic Analysis Exercise

### Victim Host
| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 | 172.16.1.66 |
| MAC | 00:1e:64:ec:f3:08 |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-SKBR25F |
| Logged-in user | ccollier |

Grounding: ARP maps 172.16.1.66 to MAC 00:1e:64:ec:f3:08 (also confirmed as `eth.src` on all frames sourced from that IP). NBNS/browser announcements give the hostname DESKTOP-SKBR25F. Kerberos `CNameString` for the same IP shows principal `ccollier` (domain-joined workstation talking to DC 172.16.1.4, domain `wiresharkworkshop.online`).

### Malware Family
**STRRAT v1.6** — **signature-confirmed**, not inferred. The malware's own C2 heartbeat is a cleartext, pipe-delimited protocol that self-identifies:

```
ping|STRRAT|1BE8292C|DESKTOP-SKBR25F|ccollier|Microsoft Windows 11 Pro|64-bit|Windows Defender|UHJvZ3JhbSBNYW5hZ2Vy|1.6|US:United States|Not Installed|<uptime>
```

(base64 field `UHJvZ3JhbSBNYW5hZ2Vy` = "Program Manager", the active window title). Bot ID `1BE8292C`, client version `1.6`. This is sent every ~5 seconds over raw TCP port 12132 with no TLS, from first beacon at t=76.99s through the end of the capture at t=585.66s (tcp.stream 83, host:port 172.16.1.66:49754 <-> 141.98.10.79:12132).

### Indicators of Compromise

| Type | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| C2 endpoint | **141.98.10.79:12132** | Sustained plaintext STRRAT ping beacon, tcp.stream 83, ~185 GB... no — 411 frames/39 kB over 508s, one continuous session |
| Malware self-ID string | `STRRAT` bot ID `1BE8292C` | Beacon payload, follow-tcp of stream 83 |

No malicious domain or malicious URL was directly captured: the C2 channel is a bare-IP raw-TCP connection with no DNS lookup preceding it and no HTTP/TLS SNI (i.e., the malware dialed the IP directly, never resolving a name for it — itself a C2 tell per the described bare-IP pattern). No file transfer or executable was observed in the clear anywhere in the capture, so **no file name or SHA256 hash can be grounded** in this evidence; none is reported.

**Circumstantial delivery context (not confirmed — TLS-encrypted, content not visible):**
Immediately before the STRRAT beacon starts (t=76.99s), the host made TLS connections to `github.com` (140.82.113.3), `objects.githubusercontent.com` (185.199.110.133), and `repo1.maven.org` (199.232.196.209) at t≈64–68s, including an 8.8 MB transfer from repo1.maven.org in 5.8 seconds. This timing is suggestive of a payload fetch shortly before infection, but the traffic is TLS-encrypted and no cleartext object was recoverable, so this is reported as behavioral context, not a confirmed delivery indicator.

**Benign context (do not treat as IOCs):**
- `ip-api.com` (208.95.112.1) GET `/json/` — plaintext HTTP geolocation lookup returning Austin, TX / Google Fiber ISP for public IP 136.49.34.127; consistent with, but not proof beyond, the malware's self-reported "US:United States" field. Common in-the-wild behavior for STRRAT and similar RATs, but ip-api.com itself is a legitimate public service, not a malicious indicator.
- All Microsoft/Windows telemetry (`*.msn.com`, `*.events.data.microsoft.com`, `login.microsoftonline.com`, Office/OneDrive endpoints, Bing, Skype, WNS), `www.msftconnecttest.com` captive-portal check, mDNS/LLMNR/SSDP chatter, Kerberos/LDAP/CLDAP/DCE-RPC/SMB2 traffic to the domain controller 172.16.1.4 — all normal enterprise/AD background noise.
- `javadl-esd-secure.oracle.com` and Maven Central lookups may reflect a legitimate JRE/JDK toolchain on the host (STRRAT itself is Java-based malware, so a JRE being present is expected but not itself malicious).

### Incident Summary
The Windows 11 workstation DESKTOP-SKBR25F (172.16.1.66, MAC 00:1e:64:ec:f3:08), logged in as user `ccollier`, was infected with **STRRAT v1.6** (bot ID 1BE8292C). Roughly one minute into the capture the host made a burst of TLS connections to GitHub/GitHub-objects and Maven Central that may represent the payload fetch, though the content is encrypted and unconfirmed. Seconds later the malware began a continuous, unencrypted heartbeat to its C2 server at **141.98.10.79:12132**, self-identifying as STRRAT and reporting host details (hostname, user, OS, Defender status, active window) every 5 seconds for the remainder of the capture. No further files, hashes, or secondary C2 channels were observed in the clear.
